s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure
did: Co-founded Chewy in 2011 and ran it out of Dania Beach Florida, selling pet food online with 1-day shipping and 24-hour human phone support; grew it to 3.5B in sales and sold it to PetSmart for 3.35B in 2017. Bought a 13 percent GameStop stake in 2020 and became chairman.
why: Pet food is heavy, low-margin and bought on a fixed refill cycle, so the winner is whoever owns the repeat order. Chewy spent venture money on overbuilt warehouses and staffed phone lines that Amazon would not fund, buying subscription behaviour in a category Amazon treated as a commodity SKU.
obst: More than 100 venture firms turned him down on the argument that Amazon would kill any online pet retailer; Chewy was still losing money in 2017 and had to sell rather than IPO, into a leveraged PetSmart buyout whose debt later traded at distressed prices.
turn: 2013, when Chewy overbuilt fulfilment capacity ahead of demand to promise 1-day delivery and revenue went from 26M to more than 200M in two years.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure
co: Duff Capital Investors / Southern Tire Mart
did: With his brother James bought back their late father's Mississippi tire dealership in 2003 and built Southern Tire Mart into the largest US commercial truck-tire dealer and retreader; folded it and 20-odd other operating businesses into Duff Capital Investors in 2007, now about 6B in revenue.
why: Fleet tires are a service contract disguised as a product. Owning retread plants plus 24-hour roadside trucks parked inside truck-stop chains made switching costs enormous for a national carrier, and the listed tire makers did not want the low-margin roadside labour that created the lock-in.
obst: Their father sold the family tire business in 1998 and the brothers spent five leveraged years buying it back; they then had to keep funding retread capacity straight through the 2008-09 freight collapse when carrier bankruptcies wiped out receivables.
turn: The 2003 repurchase of Southern Tire Mart, which gave them a platform to roll up a fragmented commercial tire market state by state.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure
did: Founded GreenSky in Atlanta in 2006, a point-of-sale lending platform letting home-improvement contractors, dentists and vets offer instant bank-funded credit at the counter; took it public in 2018 and sold it to Goldman Sachs for about 2.2B in 2022.
why: GreenSky never lent its own money. Loans were originated onto partner bank balance sheets for a fee, so it carried no credit risk and needed almost no capital, while owning the contractor relationship that a bank could never build one roof or one dental chair at a time.
obst: Zalik never finished high school and dropped out of Auburn, and was refused by venture investors for years so he bootstrapped. After the 2018 IPO the stock fell more than 80 percent amid securities-fraud suits and disputes over how loan-loss risk was disclosed.
turn: 2012, when regional banks agreed to hold GreenSky-originated paper on their own books and the company stopped needing a balance sheet.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure; fortune made in Greenwich Connecticut, resident and headquartered in Miami since 2018
did: Founded Starwood Capital in 1991 buying distressed apartment portfolios from the Resolution Trust Corporation, assembled the Sheraton and Westin chains into Starwood Hotels and launched the W brand in 1998; moved Starwood from Greenwich Connecticut to Miami Beach in 2018.
why: The RTC was force-selling apartment portfolios at a fraction of replacement cost with almost no bidders and no financing available. Sternlicht raised paired equity from Ziff family money, bought the assets, then converted hard real estate into hotel brands that earn management fees instead of rent.
obst: He lost the 2016 bidding contest for Starwood Hotels to Marriott; his Cano Health SPAC went bankrupt in 2024, and his flagship non-traded vehicle SREIT had to gate investor redemptions from late 2022 as withdrawals ran past the monthly cap.
turn: 1994, when buying Westin and then Sheraton turned a distressed apartment buyer into a global hotel brand owner.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026 (John Tyson and family)
m: Published list figure
did: Third-generation head of Tyson Foods; started in the hatchery at 13, ran the beef and pork side, became chairman in 1998 and CEO in 2000, and pushed through the roughly 3.2B purchase of IBP in 2001 that turned a chicken company into the largest US beef and pork processor.
why: Chicken alone is a commodity on a brutal three-year cycle. Owning beef and pork as well meant the protein cycles offset each other inside one company, and the combined kill capacity gave Tyson the power to set what it paid contract growers and cattle feeders rather than take a market price.
obst: Tyson tried to walk away from the IBP merger in 2001 and was ordered by the Delaware Chancery Court to complete it; the company later faced federal chicken price-fixing indictments of its executives and wrongful-death suits over Covid outbreaks in its plants in 2020.
turn: The June 2001 Delaware ruling forcing the IBP deal to close, which roughly doubled Tyson's revenue overnight.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure
did: Son of Cuban exiles raised in Argentina and Colombia; founded Related Group in Miami in 1979 building federally subsidised affordable housing, then pivoted to condominium towers and has developed more than 100,000 units. Bought out Stephen Ross's 25 percent stake in 2022.
why: He sold Miami condos to Latin American buyers who wanted dollars out of their own countries and would pay 50 percent deposits in cash before a shovel hit the ground. That pre-sale deposit structure meant construction was financed by buyers, not banks, so he could keep building when lenders would not lend.
obst: The 2008 crash left Related Group with unsold towers and it restructured about 1.5B of debt, handing buildings back to lenders and taking Perez close to personal ruin before Latin American cash buyers returned in 2011.
turn: 1998, when he abandoned government-subsidised housing for market-rate condos aimed at foreign cash buyers.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure
did: A UNC biostatistics professor who started consulting for drug companies out of his house and incorporated Quintiles in 1982, building the first large contract research organisation; it reached 5.7B in revenue and merged with IMS Health in 2016 to form IQVIA.
why: Pharma companies carried enormous fixed clinical-trial staff that sat idle between compounds. Quintiles rented that capacity by the study, so drug makers converted a fixed cost into a variable one, and the CRO accumulated trial data and investigator networks no single sponsor could match.
obst: He took Quintiles private in 2003 in a 1.7B buyout after the stock collapsed on a failed attempt to move into drug commercialisation, then had to relever and rebuild before returning to the market in 2013.
turn: 1996, when Quintiles listed on Nasdaq and used its stock to buy competitors, turning a consultancy into a global trial machine.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026 (Gary Chouest and family)
m: Published list figure
did: Took over his father's small Louisiana shrimp-boat and workboat operation in the 1970s and built Edison Chouest Offshore into a fleet of more than 200 offshore supply and construction vessels serving Gulf oil rigs and now offshore wind, with its own shipyards and port terminals.
why: Chouest built its own vessels in its own Louisiana shipyards instead of ordering from Korea, so it could design boats to a specific operator's rig programme and deliver in a cycle upturn while competitors waited in a yard queue. Vertical integration turned a charter business into a manufacturing one.
obst: The 2010 Macondo blowout and the deepwater drilling moratorium idled much of the Gulf fleet, and the 2015-2020 oil price collapse bankrupted most listed competitors; Chouest stayed private and self-funded to survive it.
turn: The late 1980s decision to buy and operate its own shipyards rather than order vessels from third-party builders.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure: about 800M from royalties and touring, 600M catalogue value, 110M real estate
did: Signed to Nashville's Big Machine at 15 and wrote or co-wrote her own songs from the start, keeping publishing. After her master recordings were sold in 2019 she re-recorded the first six albums from 2021 and bought the originals back in May 2025; the Eras Tour grossed more than 2B.
why: She owned the compositions even when she did not own the masters, so re-recording was legally hers to do and every sync licence, playlist and advert could be redirected to the version she controlled. That devalued the asset her buyer held and let her repurchase it.
obst: Big Machine sold her masters to Scooter Braun in 2019 without letting her bid; she publicly fought the sale, was told she could not perform her old songs at the 2019 AMAs, and had to spend four years re-cutting six albums to break the lock.
turn: November 2021, when Red (Taylor's Version) outsold the original and proved re-recording could kill the value of the masters she did not own.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026 (Harrison and family)
m: Published list figure; about 15 percent economic stake with majority voting control of Coca-Cola Consolidated
did: Fourth-generation head of Coca-Cola Consolidated, the bottler his great-grandfather started in 1902; joined on delivery routes in 1977, became CEO in 1994 and absorbed most of Coca-Cola's abandoned company-owned US territories between 2013 and 2017 to triple the company's size.
why: Coca-Cola decided to exit its own bottling and refranchise the territories, and Consolidated was one of very few bottlers with the balance sheet and the family control to absorb them fast. Bottling is a licensed local monopoly, so buying territory is buying a permanent geographic annuity.
obst: The refranchising deals loaded Consolidated with debt and low-margin territory just as sugary-drink volumes fell and the company had to absorb the acquired system's cost structure; his son James died in 2010 doing relief work in Kenya.
turn: 2013, when Consolidated signed the first territory-exchange agreement with The Coca-Cola Company and began quadrupling its footprint.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure
did: A former elementary school teacher and daughter of Holocaust survivors, she took over The InterTech Group as chair and CEO when her husband Jerry Zucker died in 2008 and has run the Charleston-based specialty chemicals, aerospace engineering and real estate group to about 3B in revenue.
why: InterTech buys unglamorous industrial niches with technical barriers, keeps them private and never reports quarterly, so it can hold assets through cycles that force listed chemical companies to divest. Family control is the competitive instrument, not just the ownership form.
obst: Her husband died of brain cancer in 2008 weeks before the financial crisis, leaving her to run a sprawling private industrial group she had never led, while InterTech was still digesting the contested 1.5B takeover of Canada's Lydall and BFGoodrich assets.
turn: 2008, when she moved from schoolteacher and company director to chair and chief executive on her husband's death and kept the group intact rather than selling it off.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure; one of the Holding siblings who together hold about 20 percent of First Citizens BancShares
did: A Holding-family shareholder in First Citizens BancShares, the Raleigh bank her grandfather Robert Powell Holding joined in 1918 and ran from 1935. The family's roughly 20 percent stake multiplied as First Citizens bought failed banks from the FDIC and then took over Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
why: First Citizens kept a fortress balance sheet and dual-class family control, which let it act as the FDIC's preferred buyer of failed banks. Buying deposits at a discount with loss-sharing from the government is the cheapest funding in banking, and only an overcapitalised bank is allowed to do it.
obst: Family-controlled banks were pushed hard by activists and regulators to break the dual-class structure; the March 2023 SVB purchase forced the bank to absorb 72B of assets and a fleeing venture-deposit base inside a single weekend.
turn: March 2023, when First Citizens bought Silicon Valley Bank from the FDIC and the share price roughly doubled in a day.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure
did: Took over a backyard lumber-treating plant in Abbeville Alabama with 22,000 dollars of 1971 sales and built Great Southern Wood Preserving into the largest US producer of pressure-treated pine, near 2B in annual sales, marketed under the YellaWood brand he fronted himself as the cowboy Yella Fella.
why: Treated lumber is a commodity nobody brands, so Rane branded it. Spending on television westerns starring himself gave contractors and homeowners a name to ask for at Home Depot and Lowe's, which turned a price-taking sawmill product into a shelf-position asset the retailers had to stock.
obst: He is a lawyer who inherited a failing plant and had to run it while practising law; the business nearly went under in the early 1980s when interest rates and a housing collapse froze lumber demand, and later survived the arsenic-treatment phase-out that forced a total chemistry change in 2003.
turn: 1990, when he began running the Yella Fella television campaigns and turned commodity treated pine into a branded retail product.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published list figure
did: Wrote and self-produced gospel-circuit stage plays from 1992, created the Madea franchise that has grossed more than 660M, and kept 100 percent ownership of everything he writes; built Tyler Perry Studios on a 330-acre former army base in Atlanta with 12 sound stages.
why: He financed his own productions so he never gave up the library, and he shot fast and cheap in Georgia under a 30 percent transferable tax credit. Owning the negative plus the studio means every Netflix, Amazon and BET+ deal is a licence, not a work-for-hire fee.
obst: His first six years of self-funded plays lost money and he was homeless for periods in Atlanta before House of Payne; critics and Spike Lee attacked the Madea character as minstrelsy, and studios refused to give him ownership terms until he proved the audience himself.
turn: 2005, when Diary of a Mad Black Woman opened at number one and Lionsgate agreed to distribute films he financed and owned outright.

s: Dream Finders Homes 2025 DEF 14A: 1,610,694 Class A and 57,726,153 Class B shares beneficially owned; DFH closed 14.92 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 59,336,847 beneficially owned shares x 14.92 = 885M; Forbes carried 1.1B in March 2026 before DFH halved
did: Started Dream Finders Homes in Jacksonville in 2008 with about 500,000 dollars and built 27 houses in its first full year; took it public in January 2021 and now closes over 9,000 homes a year across eight states, and in 2026 agreed to buy Beazer Homes for about 2.2B.
why: Dream Finders options its land from third-party developers instead of owning it, so it carries almost no land on the balance sheet. That let it start in the depth of the 2008 collapse with no legacy inventory and scale on turns rather than capital while land-heavy rivals were writing down dirt.
obst: He launched a homebuilder in Florida in 2008, the worst possible year and market, with no institutional backing; DFH shares have fallen roughly 50 percent since March 2026 on housing-affordability pressure, and 17.5M of his Class B shares are pledged against a margin loan.
turn: January 2021, when the IPO gave him public equity to buy builders in Texas and the Carolinas instead of growing only organically.

s: Lamar Advertising 2026 DEF 14A: 500,183 Class A and 11,362,250 Class B beneficially owned, of which 9,000,000 are held by Reilly Family LLC; LAMR closed 150.77 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,862,433 shares held outside the family LLC plus a one-fifth interest in the LLC's 9,000,000 shares, x 150.77 = 703M
did: Took over his father's Baton Rouge billboard company in 1989, took Lamar public in 1996 and rolled up hundreds of small local outdoor operators into the largest US billboard owner; converted Lamar into a REIT in 2014 and chairs it today.
why: Billboards are permitted structures on land nobody can add to, because the 1965 Highway Beautification Act froze new roadside signs. Buying an existing operator buys irreplaceable permits, so a rollup in a supply-capped asset compounds pricing power every year without building anything.
obst: The rollup was debt-financed and Lamar entered the 2001 and 2008 advertising recessions heavily levered, with local ad spend falling faster than the national market; the family had to keep the Class B structure to stop a hostile buyer taking the permit base.
turn: 1996, when the IPO gave him public paper to buy dozens of family billboard companies that would not sell for cash.

s: HCA Healthcare Form 4 filed 12 Feb 2026: 64,842 direct plus 1,317,452 shares held via trusts, GRATs and a limited partnership; HCA closed 429.19 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,382,294 beneficially owned shares x 429.19 = 593M; excludes unvested performance awards
did: Joined HCA in 1983 as a financial analyst in Nashville, ran its Western Group and became chief operating officer, then chief executive in 2019; runs about 190 hospitals and has taken HCA's market value past 90B while buying back roughly a third of the shares.
why: HCA's advantage is scale inside chosen metros rather than national coverage. Owning most of the beds in Nashville, Houston or Miami sets the price with commercial insurers, and the company recycles that cash into buybacks rather than new markets, so equity comp compounds against a shrinking share count.
obst: HCA carried the debt from the 33B 2006 leveraged buyout by KKR, Bain and the Frist family for years; as CEO he faced the 2020 pandemic, returned 6B of federal Cares Act aid under public pressure, and has fought nurse-staffing and billing investigations.
turn: 2019, when he became the first chief executive of HCA who was not a Frist or an outside hire, having spent 36 years inside the company.

s: Dillard's 2025 DEF 14A: 904,300 Class A shares held personally by William Dillard II; DDS closed 621.63 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 904,300 personally held Class A shares x 621.63 = 562M; deliberately excludes the W.D. Company Class B block he controls jointly with his brothers
did: Second-generation chief executive of Dillard's since 1998, the last large family-controlled US department store chain; kept the stores, refused to chase e-commerce scale, and ran buybacks that cut the share count by more than two-thirds while the stock went from about 30 dollars in 2020 to over 600.
why: Dillard's owns roughly 90 percent of its store real estate outright, so it has almost no rent and can shut a store without a lease penalty. That let it cut promotions and inventory hard after 2020 while mall rivals had to discount to make rent, and it bought its own shrinking float with the cash.
obst: Department stores were written off as structurally dead after 2015; Dillard's was pushed by activists to spin off its real estate into a REIT and refused, and the family had to hold a controlling Class B block through a decade in which the stock badly lagged.
turn: 2020-21, when Dillard's ran inventory far below plan coming out of the pandemic, sold at full price and generated the cash that funded the buyback.

s: Walmart Form 4 filed 29 May 2026: 4,174,578 shares held directly plus 1,059,706 through trusts and plans; WMT closed 103.70 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 5,234,284 beneficially owned shares x 103.70 = 543M
did: Started as a Walmart distribution-centre hourly associate in 1984, came back after an MBA, ran merchandising and then Sam's Club and Walmart International, and has been chief executive since 2014; took Walmart's e-commerce from a rounding error to the number two US online retailer.
why: Walmart's answer to Amazon was not a website but the 4,600 stores as forward-deployed inventory, letting it offer same-day pickup and delivery from stock it already owned. Turning fixed store assets into fulfilment capacity is a cost structure Amazon had to build from scratch.
obst: He raised US wages twice in 2015-16 and the stock fell about 30 percent as investors revolted at the earnings hit; the 3.3B Jet.com purchase in 2016 was written down and shut, and Walmart wrote off multibillion-dollar failures in Britain, Japan and Brazil on his watch.
turn: October 2015, when he told investors Walmart would spend billions on wages and e-commerce and take a year of falling profit to do it.

s: Old Dominion Freight Line Form 4 filed 28 May 2026: 606,299 in his revocable trust, 481,425 in a 2025 GRAT, 1,068,636 in a 1999 irrevocable trust, 297,250 held by his wife and 178,433 in the 401(k); ODFL closed 206.47 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,632,043 shares in his own and his wife's trusts x 206.47 = 543M; excludes shares he votes only as co-trustee of his father's trusts
did: Third-generation head of Old Dominion Freight Line in Thomasville North Carolina; became chief executive in 2008 and spent the freight recession buying and building service centres, taking ODFL from a regional less-than-truckload carrier to the most profitable one in the country.
why: LTL is a density game: an extra shipment through an already-open dock costs almost nothing. Congdon added terminal capacity in downturns when land was cheap and rivals were closing doors, so when volume returned ODFL had the network to absorb it at an operating ratio nobody else could match.
obst: He committed to building service centres through the 2008-09 freight collapse when the board could have cut capital spending, and had to hold a unionisation-free workforce against repeated Teamsters organising drives in a sector where the union sets pay.
turn: 2009, when ODFL kept opening service centres in the worst freight market in decades and took share that never went back.

s: Lamar Advertising 2026 DEF 14A: 165,035 Class A and 10,557,835 Class B beneficially owned, of which 9,000,000 are held by Reilly Family LLC; LAMR closed 150.77 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,722,870 shares held outside the family LLC plus a one-fifth interest in the LLC's 9,000,000 shares, x 150.77 = 531M
did: Joined the family billboard company in 1987 after a term in the Louisiana legislature, ran acquisitions during the 1990s rollup and became chief executive in 2011; converted Lamar into a real estate investment trust in 2014 and pushed the conversion of static boards to digital faces.
why: The REIT conversion re-rated the whole company: billboards are structures on land, so Lamar could stop paying corporate tax and pay out cash instead, which lowered its cost of capital below every non-REIT bidder for the small operators it kept buying.
obst: Getting the IRS to accept billboards as qualifying real property took a two-year private-letter-ruling fight, and digital conversion required replacing thousands of faces at over 200,000 dollars each while local advertisers were still recovering from 2009.
turn: 2014, when the IRS ruling cleared Lamar to become a REIT and the tax shield turned into an acquisition advantage.

s: Ingles Markets 2025 DEF 14A: 4,278,134 shares, 96.1 percent of Class B and 72.5 percent of total voting power; IMKTA closed 84.94 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 4,278,134 shares convertible one-for-one into Class A x 84.94 = 363M
did: Runs Ingles Markets, the Asheville grocery chain his father Robert Ingle founded in 1963; became chairman and chief executive after his father's death in 2011 and holds 96 percent of the Class B stock, controlling a 5.4B-revenue chain of about 200 supermarkets across the southern Appalachians.
why: Ingles owns nearly all its stores and most of the shopping centres around them, plus its own milk plant and fuel stations. In small Appalachian towns there is room for one supermarket, so owning the real estate keeps a national chain from opening across the street.
obst: Hurricane Helene devastated western North Carolina in September 2024, flooding stores and the company's Black Mountain headquarters and distribution centre; the chain also carries heavy real-estate debt that public-market investors persistently discount.
turn: 2011, when his father died and he inherited both the Class B control block and a chain that had just finished a decade of rebuilding its stores.

s: Forbes 2026 Top Creators list, 23 Jun 2026
m: Published list figure; Beast Industries has taken venture money at about a 5B valuation
did: Started posting YouTube videos from Greenville North Carolina at 13 and turned MrBeast into the largest channel in the world at over 640 million subscribers, then built Beast Industries around it: Feastables chocolate, Lunchly, the Beast Games series for Amazon, and the Step teen fintech app bought in February 2026.
why: He reinvested essentially all ad revenue into production budgets, so each video cost more and out-spectacled everyone else, which the recommendation algorithm rewarded with more reach. The loop only works if you refuse to take profit, and almost no creator would.
obst: He spent six years posting to almost nobody before the format worked; the 2024 Beast Games production drew lawsuits from contestants alleging injuries and unsafe conditions, and Feastables faced consumer suits over cocoa sourcing claims.
turn: 2017, when he posted himself counting to 100,000 and the stunt-spending format found its audience.

s: Aflac Form 4 filed 24 Feb 2026: 685,848 direct, 941,326 through a partnership, 908,632 as trustee for children and 5,072 held by spouse; AFL closed 116.07 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,540,878 beneficially owned shares x 116.07 = 295M
did: Second-generation chief executive of Aflac in Columbus Georgia since 1990; built the supplemental cancer and accident insurer into a company earning most of its money in Japan, and in 1999 put the Aflac Duck on US television, which took American name recognition from about 12 percent to over 90.
why: Supplemental policies are sold at the worksite through payroll deduction, so the employer does the collection and the churn is far lower than individual insurance. Aflac got the Japanese cancer-insurance licence in 1974 and held a near-monopoly there for decades under regulatory protection.
obst: Aflac's earnings are mostly yen, and repeated yen devaluations have cut reported profit regardless of operations; the company also faced a 2018 short-seller and press campaign alleging it misled its independent sales agents about earnings.
turn: 1999, when the Aflac Duck advertising campaign turned an unknown Georgia insurer into a household name and US sales tripled over the following decade.

s: Last Bank of the Ozarks Form 4 on file, 9 May 2017: 5,963,547 shares across direct holdings, the Gleason Trust, a 401(k) and family trusts; OZK closed 49.42 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 5,963,547 shares from the most recent Form 4 x 49.42 = 295M; share count is dated, current holdings are likely higher
did: Bought control of a single-branch Arkansas bank with about 28M in assets in 1979 at the age of 25, using borrowed money, and built Bank OZK into a roughly 38B-asset lender that is now one of the largest construction lenders in the United States.
why: Bank OZK lends on big-city construction projects at low loan-to-cost with the sponsor's equity in first, underwritten centrally in Little Rock rather than by local relationship officers. Low deposit costs from rural Arkansas branches funded Manhattan and Miami towers at a spread nobody local could match.
obst: A 2018 write-off of two South Carolina and North Carolina construction loans knocked the stock down about 25 percent in a day; short sellers including Carson Block have repeatedly argued the construction book is mismarked, and the bank was cut off from correspondent growth during the 2008 crisis.
turn: 2003, when he moved the bank from Arkansas commercial lending into large national real estate construction finance.

s: Target's disclosed 550M all-cash acquisition of Shipt, announced 6 Dec 2017, against roughly 65M of venture funding raised
m: Estimated majority founder stake of the 550M price, net of tax and dilution; the exact ownership share was never disclosed, so this is a modelled figure
did: Founded Shipt in Birmingham Alabama in 2014, a membership grocery-delivery service that started with Publix in Birmingham and Tampa and grew to 70 US markets; sold it to Target for 550M in cash in December 2017, then founded the furnished-apartment network Landing in 2019.
why: Shipt launched in southern cities Instacart ignored, where grocers had no delivery at all and no rival was bidding up shopper pay. It signed regional chains such as Publix and Winn-Dixie as partners rather than scraping them, so the retailer helped market the service instead of fighting it.
obst: He was rejected repeatedly by Silicon Valley investors for building outside a coastal hub and funded early growth himself after an earlier prepaid-card venture; Shipt then had to survive Instacart's entry into the South with far deeper capital.
turn: December 2017, when Target bought Shipt outright for cash rather than partnering, three years after launch.

s: Priority Technology Holdings Form 4 filed 9 Feb 2026: 34,002,878 shares held directly plus 12,500,000 indirect; PRTH closed 5.61 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 46,502,878 beneficially owned shares x 5.61 = 261M
did: Recapitalised the Georgia merchant acquirer Priority Payment Systems in 2014, took it public through a SPAC in 2018 and rebuilt it as Priority Technology, combining card acquiring with banking-as-a-service and B2B payables; the company now runs about 1B in revenue from Alpharetta.
why: Priority sells through independent software vendors and payment facilitators rather than a direct sales force, so distribution cost is someone else's. Adding a bank-account layer under the acquiring business lets it hold merchant balances and earn on the float as well as the interchange spread.
obst: His previous firm ICP Asset Management settled SEC charges in 2012 over CDO trades, and he came into payments with that record; Priority's 2018 SPAC listing left it heavily indebted and the stock has fallen more than a quarter over the past year.
turn: 2021, when the 425M purchase of Finxera added licensed money-transmission and banking rails on top of a commodity card-acquiring business.

s: SEC insider-holding filings across Eshelman-chaired issuers, 2025-2026, aggregating roughly 200M to 230M in disclosed positions
m: Sum of disclosed beneficial positions in listed companies he chairs or backs, plus proceeds from the 3.9B 2011 PPD buyout in which he was the largest individual holder
did: A pharmacist who founded Pharmaceutical Product Development in Wilmington North Carolina in 1985 and built it into a contract research organisation that ran clinical trials for most of the industry; it was taken private for 3.9B in 2011. He then founded Furiex and Eshelman Ventures.
why: PPD moved trials out of academic medical centres and into networks of community physicians, which recruited patients faster and cheaper. Speed to database lock is worth more to a sponsor than the trial fee, because every month of patent life recovered is pure margin on the drug.
obst: He was forced into a proxy fight with PPD's board in 2011 over the direction of the company he founded before the Carlyle and Hellman and Friedman buyout; his later 2.5M funding of an election-fraud investigation in 2020 produced no findings and a public legal fight to get the money back.
turn: 1996, when PPD's listing and its acquisition of Belmont Research gave it the data infrastructure to run global trials rather than US ones.

s: Home BancShares Form 4 filed 4 Jun 2026: 5,768,826 direct plus restricted and performance shares, 865,360 held by his wife and holdings in an IRA, a 401(k) and Capital Buyers; HOMB closed 30.27 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 7,166,908 beneficially owned shares x 30.27 = 217M
did: Co-founded Home BancShares in Conway Arkansas in 1998 with a group of local investors, took it public in 2006 and rolled up more than 20 failed and struggling banks across Arkansas, Florida, Alabama and Texas to build a roughly 23B-asset lender.
why: Home BancShares bought Florida banks from the FDIC after 2008 with loss-sharing agreements, so the government absorbed the bad loans and it kept the deposits and branches at a discount. Buying franchise value while carrying almost none of the credit risk is the cheapest growth in banking.
obst: He started a bank at 52 after selling an earlier one, then bet the company on distressed Florida acquisitions in 2010 when Florida real estate was still falling; the 2022 Happy Bancshares merger in Texas came just before deposit costs spiked across the sector.
turn: 2010, when the FDIC-assisted purchases of failed Florida banks gave Home BancShares a coastal franchise it could never have built branch by branch.

s: Sanderson Farms Form 4 filed 26 Jul 2022 showing his position cashed out in the merger; the Cargill and Continental Grain buyout closed at 203.00 per share
m: Peak disclosed holding of 718,587 shares x the 203.00 merger price = 146M, plus disclosed earlier sales and ESOP allocations
did: Third-generation head of Sanderson Farms in Laurel Mississippi; became president in 1984 and chief executive in 1989, and took the company from a small regional processor to the third-largest US chicken producer before selling it to Cargill and Continental Grain for 4.53B in 2021.
why: Sanderson built one new complex at a time, each fully paid for in cash before the next, and refused to carry debt through the chicken cycle. When feed costs spiked or prices collapsed, leveraged competitors sold plants and Sanderson bought growers and market share at the bottom.
obst: He publicly refused to move to antibiotic-free or no-hormone labelling when Tyson and Perdue did, and took years of activist and retailer pressure for it; the company was also named in the federal broiler price-fixing litigation that produced hundreds of millions in industry settlements.
turn: August 2021, when Cargill and Continental Grain agreed to buy the company for 4.53B in cash, the largest US poultry deal in years.

s: Bank of America Form 4 filed 18 Aug 2026: 2,699,612 shares held directly, 100,000 in trust and 3,623 in the 401(k); BAC closed 61.69 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,803,235 beneficially owned shares x 61.69 = 173M; excludes unvested restricted stock units
did: A lawyer who joined Fleet Financial in 1993 and came to Bank of America through the 2004 FleetBoston merger; became chief executive in Charlotte in January 2010 with the bank carrying Countrywide and Merrill Lynch, and spent the next decade paying out more than 80B in crisis-era legal settlements.
why: He shrank the bank rather than grew it, selling non-core units and cutting the balance sheet until the deposit franchise itself was the asset. A vast low-cost retail deposit base is the only durable funding advantage in banking, and he traded growth for it for a decade.
obst: He inherited Countrywide's mortgage liabilities and Merrill's trading book, was forced to withdraw a dividend increase in 2011 after failing a Federal Reserve stress test, and had the chairman title stripped by shareholders in 2009 before regaining it in 2014.
turn: 2011, when the 8.5B Countrywide mortgage settlement and the Buffett 5B preferred investment stopped the run on the stock.

s: LendingTree Form 4 filed 2 Oct 2025: 2,220,483 shares across direct holdings, four Lebda Family Holdings entities, a revocable trust and spousal shares; TREE closed 30.82 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,220,483 shares x 30.82 = 68M, plus a decade of disclosed Form 4 sales made when TREE traded between 200 and 400 dollars
did: Founded LendingTree in Charlotte in 1996 after a frustrating mortgage application, building the first online marketplace where lenders bid for a borrower; sold it to IAC for 734M in 2003, ran IAC operations, then took LendingTree public again as a spinoff in 2008 and still runs it.
why: LendingTree gets paid for the lead, not the loan, so it has no credit risk and no balance sheet. Its moat is the cost of buying the borrower's attention at the search auction, which is why it spends most of its revenue on marketing and why nobody has been able to undercut it at scale.
obst: He raised money in 1997 at the very edge of the dotcom window and nearly ran out before the IPO; LendingTree spent the 2008-2011 period in litigation over its own defunct mortgage-origination arm, and TREE has lost roughly half its market value in the past year.
turn: 2008, when IAC spun LendingTree back out as an independent public company and he was able to run it as a pure marketplace again.

s: Sonic Automotive 2026 DEF 14A: 1,336,528 Class A shares held personally; SAH closed 77.45 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,336,528 personally held Class A shares x 77.45 = 104M; excludes the Sonic Financial Corporation Class B block he shares with his siblings
did: Son of NASCAR track builder O. Bruton Smith; joined Sonic Automotive in 1995, became chief executive in 2018 and runs about 110 franchised dealerships plus the EchoPark used-car chain and a powersports arm, on roughly 15B of revenue out of Charlotte.
why: Franchised dealers hold state-protected territorial rights that manufacturers cannot revoke, which makes the franchise itself a licensed asset. Sonic bet that adding a no-haggle used-car format on top of that protected base would let it buy trade-ins from its own service lanes instead of at auction.
obst: EchoPark lost hundreds of millions as used-car prices collapsed after 2022 and Sonic had to close stores and take impairments; the family also had to fund the take-private of Speedway Motorsports in 2019 while carrying dealership floorplan debt.
turn: 2018, when he took over as chief executive and pushed capital into EchoPark rather than more new-car franchises.

s: Cal-Maine Foods Schedule 13D/A filed 5 Aug 2025: 1,466,586 shares, 3.02 percent of the common stock; CALM closed 82.80 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,466,586 shares x 82.80 = 121M, plus proceeds from the family's 2025 secondary sale of converted Class A stock
did: Married the founder's daughter, joined Cal-Maine Foods in Mississippi in 1980, became chief executive in 1997 and chairman in 2012, and rolled up regional egg producers until Cal-Maine supplied about a fifth of the shell eggs sold in the United States.
why: Eggs are the most commoditised food there is, so the only lever is cost per dozen and proximity to the retailer's distribution centre. Cal-Maine bought family farms near the big grocery chains, consolidated a fragmented industry no one else wanted, and let avian-influenza supply shocks do the pricing.
obst: Cal-Maine was found liable in 2023 for egg price-fixing in a jury verdict brought by food manufacturers, and repeated avian-influenza outbreaks have forced the culling of millions of its hens; the founder's family converted and sold down its supervoting Class A block in 2025.
turn: April 2025, when the founder's Daughters LLC converted its entire 4.8M-share Class A block and ended the dual-class structure that had controlled the company.

s: Dillard's 2025 DEF 14A: 450,373 Class A shares beneficially owned; DDS closed 621.63 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 450,373 Class A shares x 621.63 = 280M; excludes any interest in the W.D. Company holding vehicle
did: Daughter of the founder William Dillard Sr; joined the company in 1970 and spent five decades as an executive vice president over merchandising and the womens apparel divisions, sitting on the board of the last large family-controlled US department store chain.
why: Dillard's buying is centralised in Little Rock and the merchandising executives are family, so markdown discipline is a family decision rather than a quarterly one. That is why the chain could hold price through 2021 while public-market rivals discounted to make rent, and why the share count could be bought in.
obst: She spent her career inside a sector written off as terminally declining, in a company that refused analysts' demands to spin off real estate or chase e-commerce, and had to hold family stock through a decade in which the stock badly lagged the market.
turn: 2020-21, when Dillard's deliberately under-bought inventory coming out of the pandemic, sold at full margin and the shares went from about 30 dollars to over 400.
